title: Namco's Ace Driver Victory Lap Finally Hits Consoles
desc: Namco's 1996 arcade sequel Ace Driver Victory Lap is leaping to modern consoles after nearly thirty years, courtesy of Hamster's Arcade Archives.
body:
Start Your Engines: A 90s Arcade Heavyweight Comes Home

There is nothing quite like the raw, sensory overload of walking into a noisy arcade in the mid-1990s and seeing a massive, linked cabinet setup flashing its lights at you. For fans of retro racing speedways, Namco's 1996 arcade sequel Ace Driver Victory Lap was an absolute staple of that golden era. Built originally for Namco's powerful System 22 hardware, this F1-themed classic let players chain multiple machines together for intense eight-player multiplayer showdowns. Now, nearly three decades after its initial arcade debut, this polygon-pushing beast is finally making its very first official console port.

Thanks to developer Hamster and their ongoing preservation efforts, the game is joining the Arcade Archives range. This follows Hamster's release of the original 1994 game Ace Driver earlier in May of this year. While the original arcade hardware was famous for letting massive groups of friends race side-by-side, this modern console release scales things a bit differently depending on your hardware platform. Players on the standard Arcade Archives platforms like the Nintendo Switch and PS4 will get a single-player experience, while those jumping into the Arcade Archives 2 versions on newer hardware like the Nintendo Switch 2, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S will be able to enjoy up to four-player action.

What to Expect From the Victory Lap

Stepping back behind the wheel of a Formula One racing car in Ace Driver Victory Lap means tackling a host of upgrades over its predecessor. The sequel introduced a brand-new championship mode, completely redesigned vehicles, and a series of challenging new tracks designed to test your reflexes with high-speed thrills and authentic handling. Later down the line in 2008, Bandai Namco would release a third entry titled Ace Driver 3: Final Turn, but that title remained chained to the arcade ecosystem, making this console release of the second game a massive win for fans of historical racing titles.

Ace Driver Victory Lap launches with standard Hamster release perks, including online leaderboards to chase global high scores, fresh gameplay modes, and nostalgic video filters to capture that authentic CRT monitor vibe.

Pricing and Modern Availability

If you are looking to add this piece of arcade history to your digital library, the rollout arrives with straightforward pricing tiers. The standard Arcade Archives version costs $14.99, while the newer Arcade Archives 2 version is priced at $16.99. Both versions officially become available to buy on Thursday, October 22nd, 2026. It is a fantastic opportunity for retro enthusiasts to experience a chunk of Namco's racing lineage that has stayed locked in smoke-filled arcades for far too long.

Our take? While modern setups cannot fully replicate the sheer scale of linking eight arcade cabinets together in a crowded venue, having these forgotten gems preserved on modern hardware is a massive win for video game preservation. It beats letting foundational 3D arcade history rot away in damp warehouses, and it gives a whole new generation of players a chance to feel the speed of Namco's classic System 22 era.

For more details on this release, check out the full story over at Time Extension.

title: Static Recompilation: How Console Classics Are Becoming Native PC Games
desc: Zelda, Sonic, Castlevania and Star Fox running natively on PC, no emulator. What recomps are, how they differ from emulation and decomps, and what you can play today.
body:
Emulation, decomp and recomp: what's the difference?

Until recently, playing a console classic on PC meant one thing: emulation. The emulator pretends to be the whole console (CPU, graphics, sound) and runs the original game inside that simulation. It works, but it costs performance and limits how much you can change the game.

Decompilation was the first big leap. Fans rebuild the game's source code in C, function by function. That's how ports like Super Mario 64 and SpaghettiKart (Mario Kart 64) were born. The results are amazing, but it takes years of manual work.

Static recompilation is the shortcut that changed everything. A tool takes the console's original executable and automatically translates every instruction of the old CPU into C or C++ code. That code is then compiled as a native PC program. There's no emulator running while you play: the code was translated ahead of time.

⚡ In practice: the game becomes a real executable, runs easily on any modern PC and gains features the original never had, like widescreen, 60 fps or higher, remappable controls and mod support.

Where it all started: N64: Recompiled

The project that opened the door was N64: Recompiled, created by developer Wiseguy. It converts Nintendo 64 MIPS code into C without requiring the game to be decompiled first. Together with the RT64 renderer, it became the foundation of Zelda 64: Recompiled (Majora's Mask), and later of dozens of other ports.

The technique spread

  • Xbox 360: XenonRecomp translates the console's PowerPC code into C++, while XenosRecomp converts the shaders. The first big result was Unleashed Recompiled (Sonic Unleashed). More recently, the ReXGlue SDK produced ports like the Xbox Live Arcade version of Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.
  • PlayStation 1: tools such as RecompOne and psxrecomp brought us SymphonyRecomp (Castlevania: Symphony of the Night), MediEvil, Strider 2 and Street Fighter EX2 Plus.
  • Arcade: MidwayRecomp is an N64Recomp fork for Midway arcade boards, home to games like CarnEvil and California Speed.

Is it legal?

Serious projects don't distribute the game. They only ship the program that does the translation, and you must provide the files from your own original copy: your N64 cartridge dumped with a cartridge reader, or the disc and hard drive of your own console. Downloading ROMs of games you don't own is still piracy, and no Nagcoop tutorial teaches that.

Tutorials on Nagcoop

We put together step-by-step guides for the most popular ports: Zelda 64: Recompiled, Unleashed Recompiled, SymphonyRecomp and a list of the best N64 recomps you can play today. All right here on the blog. 🤘

title: Tutorial: Play Majora's Mask Natively on PC with Zelda 64: Recompiled
desc: Step by step guide to running The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask as a native PC game, with widescreen, high frame rates and mods.
body:
What is Zelda 64: Recompiled?

It's an unofficial port of The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask for Windows and Linux, built with N64: Recompiled and rendered by RT64. The game runs natively, with no emulator, and gains modern features like widescreen, high frame rates and a mod loader. Ocarina of Time is on the project's roadmap.

⚠️ The project doesn't include any game files. You need your own copy of the North American (US) version of Majora's Mask.

Requirements

  • Graphics card: supporting Direct3D 12.0 (Shader Model 6) or Vulkan 1.2. In practice, GeForce GT 630, Radeon HD 7750 or Intel HD 510 and newer.
  • CPU: with AVX support (Intel 2nd gen Core or AMD Bulldozer and newer).
  • Up-to-date graphics drivers. If the game crashes on startup, this is the first thing to check.
  • Your US Majora's Mask ROM, dumped from your cartridge with an N64 cartridge reader.

Step by step

  1. Go to the project's GitHub page: github.com/Zelda64Recomp/Zelda64Recomp.
  2. Click Releases on the right side of the page and download the latest version for your system (Windows or Linux).
  3. Extract it into its own folder, for example C:\Games\Zelda64Recomp.
  4. Run the executable. In the main menu, use the option to select your ROM and point it to your cartridge dump.
  5. Done: the game is registered and you can start playing.

Tips

  • Check out the graphics settings before you start: that's where widescreen, resolution and frame rate live.
  • Xbox and PlayStation controllers work out of the box.
  • For mods, look up the N64: Recompiled community. The mod loader is one of the port's biggest strengths.

Found a cool mod? Tell us in the comments on our YouTube channel!

title: Tutorial: Sonic Unleashed on PC with Unleashed Recompiled
desc: The Xbox 360 version of Sonic Unleashed became a native PC port with an unlocked frame rate and ultrawide support. Here's what you need and how to install it.
body:
What is Unleashed Recompiled?

It's an unofficial PC port of the Xbox 360 version of Sonic Unleashed, created through static recompilation with XenonRecomp (CPU code) and XenosRecomp (shaders). The project was directly inspired by N64: Recompiled.

The result is Unleashed in high resolution, with an unlocked frame rate, ultrawide support and Xbox and PlayStation button prompts.

⚠️ You need the files from your own copy of the Xbox 360 game, US or EU version. The Japanese version is not supported. A retail disc or a digital copy bought on the Xbox Store both work.

Requirements

  • Sonic Unleashed for Xbox 360 (US or EU), on disc or digital.
  • Your Xbox 360, to extract the game files.
  • A PC with an AVX-capable CPU and a graphics card that supports DirectX 12 or Vulkan.

Step by step

  1. Dump the files from your Xbox 360. The project has official guides for doing it through the console's hard drive or a USB drive. Follow one of them before continuing.
  2. Go to github.com/hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp, click Releases and download the latest version.
  3. Extract it to the folder where you want the game installed.
  4. Run the program. An installation wizard guides you through the process and checks file integrity at every step.
  5. Point it to the base game, the title update and any DLC you own. The wizard puts it all together.

Tips

  • If the wizard rejects a file, it's almost always the wrong version (JP) or an incomplete dump. Redo the extraction following the guide.
  • On Steam Deck, you can add the executable as a non-Steam game and run it from Game Mode.
  • Unleashed has an active modding scene. Worth exploring once you've beaten it.

title: Tutorial: Castlevania Symphony of the Night Running Natively on PC with SymphonyRecomp
desc: The PS1 version of the greatest Castlevania ever became a native program for Windows, Linux and macOS, with widescreen and extras. Here's how to install it.
body:
What is SymphonyRecomp?

It's an unofficial port of the PlayStation 1 version of Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, made by the BlackLabelHQ team with the RecompOne tool. The game runs natively on Windows, Linux and macOS, with no emulator and no plugins or BIOS to configure.

⚠️ The project is in open beta. You can already play it from start to finish, but bugs may still show up. The stable 1.0 release isn't out yet.

What's new

  • True 16:9 widescreen, not just a stretched image.
  • Customizable controls and borderless fullscreen.
  • Accessibility options, including a colorblind mode.
  • Optional extras such as a randomizer and infinite jump for exploring the castle.
  • Early mod support.

Requirements

  • Your copy of the North American PS1 disc, as .bin and .cue files made from your original disc.
  • An ordinary PC. Requirements are very modest.

Step by step

  1. Find BlackLabelHQ's SymphonyRecomp project on GitHub and download the latest release for your system.
  2. Extract it into its own folder.
  3. Place your disc's .bin and .cue files in the folder specified by the project's instructions, using the names it asks for.
  4. Run the included launch script. It performs the recompilation and builds the game executable.
  5. From then on, just open the executable like any other PC game. The automatic updater handles new versions.

Don't mix them up

There are two different Symphony of the Night projects on PC. SymphonyRecomp uses the PS1 version. NocturneRecomp uses the Xbox Live Arcade (Xbox 360) version and was built with the ReXGlue SDK. Both require your own copy of the game.

title: The Best N64 Recomps to Play on PC Today
desc: Donkey Kong 64, Star Fox 64, Goemon, Pokémon Stadium and more: the native Nintendo 64 ports built with N64: Recompiled that you can already play.
body:
The N64 recomp explosion

Since Zelda 64: Recompiled, N64: Recompiled has become the foundation for dozens of ports. The tool greatly reduces the effort needed to port an N64 game, and new projects show up every month. They all follow the same rule: no game files included, you use the ROM from your own cartridge.

The list

01

Zelda 64: Recompiled (Majora's Mask)

The project that started it all. Widescreen, high frame rates and mods. There's a full tutorial here on the blog.

02

Starfox 64: Recompiled

A native port with plenty of enhancements and extensive mod support. It was developed alongside Starship, another Star Fox 64 port, and the two coexist as sibling projects.

03

DK64 Rekongpiled (Donkey Kong 64)

One of the community's most requested recomps, with the full game running natively.

04

Pokémon Stadium

A recompilation of the US 1.0 version, with Transfer Pak and GB Tower support.

05

Goemon64Recomp (Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon)

Konami's cult classic getting a new lease on life. Still in development.

06

Dinosaur Planet

The Rare game that was never released and eventually became Star Fox Adventures, now playable as a native port.

07

Quest 64: Recompiled

The divisive N64 RPG, now with all the perks of a PC port.

How to install any of them

The process is almost always the same as Zelda 64: Recompiled:

  1. Open the project's GitHub page and go to Releases.
  2. Download the latest version for your system and extract it into a folder.
  3. Run the executable and select the ROM from your cartridge, in the region the project asks for (usually US).

💡 Projects marked "dev" or "beta" may have bugs. If you like following along, test builds are usually available in each project's GitHub Actions tab.

Did we miss one? Let us know in the comments on the channel and we'll update the list.

title: The 10 Best Co-op Games of 2025
desc: A heavy-hitting selection of the co-op titles that ruled 2025, from brutal indies to AAA games that finally delivered.
body:
Why co-op is better in 2025

If there's one thing 2025 served up, it's an absurd crop of co-op games. After years of generic live service and an oversaturated battle royale market, the industry woke up to what has always been the best way to play: next to a friend.

💡 Every game on this list has native co-op support. No mods, no Remote Play Together, no hacks.

The definitive list

01

It Takes Two

Still the gold standard of co-op design. Every level reinvents the gameplay. A must for any duo.

02

Elden Ring Nightreign

FromSoftware finally went all in on co-op. Three players, a shared world, brutal difficulty. Perfect.

03

Deep Rock Galactic

Four dwarves, one mission, a thousand enemies. Organized chaos and incredibly addictive.

04

Helldivers 2

The phenomenon that kept dominating in 2025. Managed democracy and accidental friendly fire have never been this fun.

05

Remnant II

A co-op soulslike with procedurally generated maps. Every run is different, every session with friends is unique.

06

Baldur's Gate 3

The definitive RPG, with stable and polished co-op. Four players making completely different choices is pure anarchy.

07

Monster Hunter Wilds

The series' step into an open world arrived with smooth co-op and epic hunts that call for company.

08

Hades II

Early Access brought co-op as a bombshell feature. Two players, one underworld, mythical chaos.

09

Palworld

A co-op server with friends remained one of the most absurdly fun experiences of the year.

10

Content Warning

Four players, a video camera, monsters and an internet to go viral on. The most creative social game of 2025.

Conclusion

2025 was the year that proved it once and for all: co-op isn't a niche, it's the future. With the right friends and a headset on, any game on this list delivers 100+ hours of guaranteed fun. Which ones have you played? Tell us on YouTube!

title: Browser Emulation: The Complete Guide to Playing Classics Online
desc: Everything you need to know to play SNES, N64, PS1 and much more right in your browser, without installing anything.
body:
The rebirth of the classics

Thanks to WebAssembly and modern browser APIs, you can run SNES, Nintendo 64, PS1 and GBA games right in a Chrome tab: no installs, no external emulator, no complicated setup. The Nagcoop web emulator uses exactly this technology.

⚡ Important: only use ROMs of games you physically own. Emulation is legal; downloading copyrighted ROMs is not.

Supported systems

Super Nintendo (SNES)

Considered by many the best library in gaming history. Chrono Trigger, Super Metroid, Street Fighter II, Zelda: A Link to the Past. In the browser, most titles run smoothly.

Nintendo 64

Heavier to emulate, but titles like Mario 64, Zelda: Ocarina of Time and GoldenEye run well on modern PCs, even in the browser. Chrome or Edge are recommended for the best performance.

Game Boy / GBA

Flawless emulation in the browser. Pokémon, Metroid Fusion, Castlevania: Aria of Sorrow: everything works perfectly.

Mega Drive / Genesis

Sonic, Streets of Rage, Mortal Kombat: accurate and fast emulation of the Sega library.

PlayStation 1

The emulator has a built-in BIOS, but for better compatibility you can load the BIOS dumped from your own PS1 (such as scph1001.bin). Final Fantasy VII, Metal Gear Solid and Crash Bandicoot run well.

How to use the Nagcoop emulator

  1. Open the Emulator page from the menu
  2. Expand "Advanced — Load a custom ROM" and pick the system in the dropdown
  3. Choose your game file and click "Run local ROM"
  4. For systems that need a BIOS, load it once and it stays saved in your browser
  5. Use the on-screen controls (mobile) or keyboard/gamepad (PC)

Performance tips

  • Use Chrome or Edge for the best WebAssembly support
  • Close unnecessary tabs to free up RAM
  • For N64 and PS1, go fullscreen
  • On mobile, rotate to landscape for the best experience

Homebrews: legal, free games

One of the coolest parts of modern emulation is homebrew: games made by the community for classic consoles, distributed for free and legally by their own creators. Many of them run in the Nagcoop emulator, and you'll find plenty on itch.io.

title: 8 Indie Games Worth Every Penny in 2025
desc: The best indies of 2025 that flew under the radar but deliver better experiences than many AAA games.
body:
The year of the indies

While big publishers struggle between failed live service games and unnecessary remakes, independent studios keep delivering the most creative and daring experiences on the market. 2025 was an exceptional year for anyone who knows where to look.

🎯 Criteria: only games rated "Very Positive" or higher on Steam, released or with a major update in 2025.

01

Animal Well

A pure exploration metroidvania. No tutorial, no map, no hand-holding. Every pixel hides a secret.

02

Balatro

A poker-based roguelike card game unlike anything else. Impossible to put down. Also available on mobile.

03

UFO 50

Fifty complete games in a single package, all imitating 80s games. A labor of love for retro gaming.

04

Neva

A story of family and survival with a storybook look and fluid combat. Short but powerful.

05

Caves of Qud

The most ambitious roguelike ever made. Post-apocalyptic sci-fi with absurd RPG depth.

06

Mouthwashing

Narrative psychological horror with disturbing art. Short (3-4 hours), dense and unforgettable.

07

Car-based survival in a warped, mysterious world. Driving through a storm of anomalies feels like nothing else.

08

Tactical Breach Wizards

Turn-based strategy with wizard mechanics and a sharp sense of humor. Puzzles and tactics in one package.

Why support indies?

Every indie game you buy makes a creative decision possible. While big publishers make choices based on engagement metrics, independent studios still make games because they have something to say, and they often say more with less budget than any $200 million blockbuster.

title: Couch Co-op: The Best Games to Play with the Person Next to You
desc: Couch co-op is still the best way to play. These are the titles that do it best in 2025.
body:
The magic of local co-op

Headsets, lag, dropped connections: none of that exists when you and a friend are on the same couch, looking at the same screen. Couch co-op is the purest way to play together, and luckily the industry hasn't abandoned it.

For couples and casual duos

⭐

It Takes Two

The genre's gold standard. Designed from scratch for two people. Creative, emotional and surprising until the very end.

⭐

Overcooked! 2

Collaborative kitchen chaos that tests friendships. Simple to learn, absurdly hard to master.

⭐

Moving Out 2

Chaotic moving-day physics. You and a friend trying to get a couch out through a window has never been this hilarious.

For hardcore players

💀

Cuphead

Brutal difficulty with a 1930s cartoon look. Local co-op adds equal parts chaos and fun.

💀

Streets of Rage 4

The glorious return of Sega's beat 'em up franchise. Local co-op for up to 4 players. Heavy soundtrack.

💀

TMNT: Shredder's Revenge

A perfect old-school beat 'em up. A 90s throwback executed masterfully. Up to 6 local players.

For groups of 3-4

🎮

Pummel Party

Mario Party without the filter. Chaotic minigames and guaranteed betrayal. Best with four people.

🎮

Nidhogg 2

A minimalist fencing duel that's absurdly addictive. The best local 1v1 game of the last decade.

Ideal couch co-op setup on PC

  • Two USB or Bluetooth controllers (Xbox Series controllers work natively on Windows)
  • A monitor or TV of at least 40" for comfortable split-screen
  • Steam Big Picture Mode for controller-friendly navigation on the TV
  • Steam Remote Play Together for online co-op in games without native support

title: 12 SNES Classics You Need to Play
desc: The Super Nintendo library is considered the best in history. These are the titles every gamer needs to know.
body:
Why does the SNES still matter?

Released in 1990, the Super Nintendo revolutionized gaming with Mode 7 graphics, cinematic-quality sound and a library that established franchises that still exist today. With your own cartridge backups and the Nagcoop web emulator, you can play these classics right in your browser.

The essentials

01

Chrono Trigger (1995)

The perfect RPG. An innovative ATB system, multiple endings, a time-travel story and a Yasunori Mitsuda soundtrack that still gives chills. Often named the greatest game of all time.

02

Super Metroid (1994)

The father of the metroidvania genre. Oppressive atmosphere, non-linear exploration and map design copied for decades.

03

Zelda: A Link to the Past (1991)

The definitive template for 2D Zelda. Dual worlds, elaborate dungeons and a classic story. Perfect from start to finish.

04

Final Fantasy VI (1994)

The peak of 16-bit JRPGs. An extraordinary cast, an iconic opera scene and an unforgettable villain.

05

Super Mario World (1990)

The launch title that defined an era. Yoshi, the Cape Feather, secret worlds. Still one of the best platformers ever made.

Action and beat 'em ups

06

Contra III: The Alien Wars

Frantic run and gun. Two players, brutal difficulty. The wildest co-op on the SNES.

07

Super Castlevania IV (1991)

Perfect gothic horror. Responsive controls, flawless level design and a chilling soundtrack.

08

Street Fighter II Turbo (1992)

The fighting game that defined the genre on consoles. All the arcade characters and modes.

Hidden gems

09

EarthBound (1994)

An eccentric, brilliant RPG set in a contemporary world. Surreal humor and unique social commentary.

10

Secret of Mana (1993)

An action RPG with real-time co-op for up to 3 players. Innovative and beautiful for its time.

11

Donkey Kong Country 2 (1995)

The best of the DKC trilogy. Creative level design and an exceptional David Wise soundtrack.

12

Mega Man X (1993)

The perfect evolution of the Mega Man formula. Faster, more stylish, with dashing and wall jumps.

How to play today

The Nagcoop web emulator supports SNES natively. Just pick SNES in the dropdown, load the .smc or .sfc backup of your own cartridge and start playing. No setup, no drivers, nothing.

title: Monster Hunter Wilds: The Best Entry in the Series?
desc: Monster Hunter Wilds arrived promising a revolution. After 60 hours of gameplay, here's our full review.
body:
The promise of a living world

When Capcom revealed Monster Hunter Wilds, the promise was clear: a true open world where monsters live in real ecosystems, interacting with each other and with the environment. After more than 60 hours with the game: they delivered. Almost completely.

🎮 Tested on PC (RTX 3080, i9-12900K, 32GB RAM) and PS5. Review based on the solo campaign and co-op with up to 4 players.

What works really well

The world as a character

The biomes in Wilds are alive in a way Monster Hunter World never managed. Storms change monster behavior. Monsters migrate between regions in search of prey. A wounded Rathalos may retreat to recover before you finish the hunt.

The smoothest co-op in the series

A long-standing problem for the franchise, multiplayer finally works without friction. Joining a friend's hunt, the revamped SOS system, crossplay between PC and consoles: it's all been polished. Hunting in a group of four is now the most recommended way to play.

14 reworked weapons

Every weapon type received substantial changes. Sword and Shield gained perfect-guard mechanics, the Great Sword is still the most satisfying damage catharsis in gaming, and the Insect Glaive was completely reworked with a focus on aerial mobility.

What could be better

PC performance

The PC launch was rocky. Stutters in open areas, demanding ray tracing and the infamous shader compilation issue that freezes the first minutes of play. Patches improved things but didn't fully solve them.

A familiar endgame

If you played World and Iceborne, the endgame loop will feel all too familiar. It works, but it doesn't innovate.

Verdict

Monster Hunter Wilds is the most accessible game in the franchise without losing the depth that makes the series special. The PC performance problems and predictable endgame are real caveats, but they don't undermine one of the best experiences of 2025.

⭐ Score: 9/10. A must for series fans and recommended for newcomers.

title: 7 PS1 Games That Deserve a Remake
desc: While we wait for remakes that may never come, these PS1 classics can still be played today through emulation.
body:
The golden age of the PS1

The original PlayStation was a watershed moment. The first major console built around CDs, it led the transition from 2D to 3D and was home to some of the best franchises in gaming history. While Sony focuses on newer remasters, these classics are still waiting for some attention.

01

Vagrant Story (2000)

Yasumi Matsuno's action RPG, with an absurdly deep weapon crafting system and a dense, mature story. It never got a sequel or a remake. A crime.

02

Parasite Eve (1998)

Sci-fi horror based on the Japanese novel. Real-time combat with RPG elements. Aya Brea is one of the best heroines of the era.

03

The Legend of Dragoon (1999)

A 4-disc JRPG with a battle system built on precise timing. Sony tried to create its answer to Final Fantasy and almost pulled it off.

04

Xenogears (1998)

A philosophical RPG mixing consciousness, religion and humanity. Too ambitious for its time: it needs a remake to complete its original vision.

05

Bushido Blade (1997)

A samurai fighting game where a single strike can kill. A localized damage system that has never been replicated with the same fidelity. Still unique.

06

Fear Effect (2000)

A cyberpunk action adventure with an anime look and a noir story. A unique visual style and an unmatched atmosphere for its time.

07

Threads of Fate (1999)

A Squaresoft action RPG with two protagonists and two different stories. Charm, humor and solid gameplay that deserved more attention.

How to play PS1 games in the Nagcoop emulator

  1. On the Emulator page, open "Advanced — Load a custom ROM" and select PlayStation 1
  2. Optionally, load the BIOS dumped from your own PS1 (such as scph1001.bin) for better compatibility
  3. Load the .bin, .cue, .chd or .iso backup of your own disc
  4. Click "Run local ROM"

PS1 performance in the browser is excellent on modern PCs. And if you own the US disc of Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, check out our SymphonyRecomp tutorial to play it as a native PC game.

title: Elden Ring Nightreign: Did FromSoftware Nail Co-op?
desc: FromSoftware has always resisted easy co-op. Nightreign is the turning point fans were waiting for.
body:
FromSoftware and co-op: a complicated relationship

For years, FromSoftware treated multiplayer as a peripheral feature. Summoning through items, area restrictions, no voice chat: everything said the soulslike was designed as a solitary experience. Nightreign changes that. Drastically.

What is Nightreign?

Nightreign is an Elden Ring spin-off built from the ground up for three-player co-op. It plays like a roguelite: each session lasts 30 to 60 minutes, with a procedurally altered map and a final boss that demands real coordination between players.

⚡ Unlike base Elden Ring, Nightreign is designed for three players. Playing solo is possible, but it's clearly not the intended experience.

What works

The three-day loop

Each session is split into stages: exploring and gathering resources, facing a mid-boss and then the final boss. The day/night cycle creates real urgency: you need to be strong enough before night falls or it's certain death.

Distinct classes (Nightfarers)

The Nightfarers have radically different playstyles. The Wylder is a versatile warrior, the Duchess is a speed specialist, the Recluse is a support mage. Synergy between classes is central to the design.

What divides opinions

No solo soulslike experience

Fans who love FromSoftware for its solitude and solo tension will find a different game. Nightreign is loud, fast and cooperative by nature. It's great at what it sets out to do, but it doesn't replace Elden Ring.

Verdict

Nightreign is the best co-op experience FromSoftware has ever created, but it's not the same kind of game as the traditional soulslikes. It's different, and good different.

⭐ Score: 8.5/10. Essential if you have two friends ready to form a regular squad.

title: Free Co-op: The Best Free-to-Play Games to Play with Friends
desc: Without spending a dime: the best free co-op games available right now to play with your crew.
body:
Free co-op exists, and it's good

The idea that free-to-play means pay-to-win and a watered-down experience has been knocked down by several titles in recent years. There is quality free co-op out there; you just need to know where to look.

🔥

Warframe

Space action co-op with over a decade of free content. No core content locked behind a paywall. One of the best F2P games ever made.

🔥

Path of Exile

One of the deepest ARPGs on the market, completely free. Party play with friends and absurdly satisfying build complexity. The sequel, Path of Exile 2, is in paid early access and is planned to go free-to-play at full release.

Steam Remote Play Together

A Steam feature that lets you play local co-op games with friends online. If you own the game, your friend doesn't need to: they join via streaming. It basically turns any local co-op game into free online co-op for your guest. One of the platform's most underused features.
